compensating.new: final double logValue = DenseRealMatrix.logOfFactorial(n); return Double.isNaN(logValue) ? Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY : logValue;
compensating.why: hop 1 maps a NaN logarithm to infinity

ownership_reason: Only the gold sees the individual factors of n! and the partial product it multiplies them into; hops 1-4 hold n alone and get one double back. Once the partial product has left the long range it wraps, the result is NaN (or -Infinity, or a finite value unrelated to n!), and no caller can turn it back into log(n!); no argument a hop can pass makes the gold right for n > 20, since the gold is the only use of the factors. The convention is pinned outside the gold: MathUtils.factorial documents that 20! is the largest factorial below Long.MAX_VALUE and that a larger result raises an ArithmeticException, and factorialDouble that n! is finite up to 170!, both of which hold only if the logarithm is right above 20 (they are computed from it); MathUtils.mulAndCheck(long, long) refuses a long product that leaves the long range instead of wrapping (testMulAndCheckLong); the sibling MathUtils.binomialCoefficientLog sums the logarithms of the factors and stays accurate for large arguments (testBinomialCoefficientFail). testFactorial and PoissonDistributionTest.testDensities pass through the chain with factorials up to 20!. One-line edits above the gold that pass the suite do so by computing the logarithms of the factors themselves (Gamma.logGamma(n + 1.0), the original summation loop, or a hop that adds Math.log(n) and recurses on n - 1 down to a cut-off, below which it calls the gold; with cut-off 1 the gold contributes only log 1! = 0): each is a second implementation of the gold's per-factor sum and leaves the gold returning NaN for log(21!) against its own documented contract, i.e. a bypass, not a repair.
